top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) credits one jointly authored body of design-based evidence on how technology and import competition reshape labour demand and local adjustment. The central claims have been re-run, challenged and replicated in other countries for more than a decade, and the debate over magnitudes is what a mature programme looks like. Omitting Dorn would misstate where the most replicable evidence came from. The citation should claim credibly identified evidence on adjustment, not a settled welfare verdict or the origin of the task framework. P003 (Katz in place of Dorn) is a defensible broader variant, but it relies more on a framework with diffuse credit and adjacency to recent prizes, so it ranks second. P002 (BLP) ranks above P004. Its methods have been stress-tested in applied work for about thirty years, although it is a method and its attribution excludes Bresnahan and Reiss. P004 ranks lower mainly because the cross-country constitutional evidence is less credibly identified, and it sits near the 2024 prize. P000 is last because a well-evidenced, mature candidate with a defensible attribution is available.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for any candidate named in the slate. Disclosed for transparency only: I am at the Stockholm School of Economics alongside other members (Andersson, Friberg, Strömberg). I co-authored in 2009 with Tore Ellingsen, a former chair, and my main co-author Magnus Johannesson is a former committee member. These are ties to members, not to candidates. My metascience background may lead me to weight replicability more heavily than others do, which is a perspective and not a conflict. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
